CALL RECORDING CONSENT CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Do you need consent to record this call?

Pick the caller's and recipient's US states and get an instant one-party vs. all-party consent determination, the exact statute cited, and a ready-to-read disclosure script for your call opening.

Nothing you pick is uploaded — this is a fixed reference table evaluated entirely in this browser. Not legal advice. See the disclaimer below before you rely on this for an actual call.

1. Check a call between two states

Caller
Recipient

2. Get a disclosure script for that requirement


    
Run "Check requirement" first — the script matches whichever result it last showed. Copy it, adapt the bracketed parts, and read it verbatim if all-party consent is required.

  


  

    
Prefer a CLI, or want this in a script?

    
Same table, zero dependencies, one file:

    
node cli.mjs check California Texas
node cli.mjs check CA TX --json
node cli.mjs states
node cli.mjs script all-party --company "Acme Inc." --purpose "training purposes"

    
Get cli.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install, no network call ever. check exits 1 when all-party consent is required, so it doubles as a one-line reminder in an onboarding or call-script build step.

  


  

    
All 51 jurisdictions

    
The fourteen all-party states are listed with their statute; every other state and DC follows the federal one-party baseline. Full table, sourced and with per-state notes on any known ambiguity: why this varies by state.

    

      
StateRuleStatute

      
    

  


  

    
Common questions

    
Is call recording consent governed by federal law or state law?

    
Both. The federal Wiretap Act (18 U.S.C. § 2511(2)(d)) sets a one-party-consent floor — a person who is a party to a call may record it without telling the other party — but a state is free to require more. Fourteen states and DC do not: California, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Montana, Nevada, New Hampshire, Oregon, Pennsylvania, and Washington require every party's consent. This tool applies the stricter of the two states whenever either side of a call is in one of those fourteen.

    
What happens if the caller and recipient are in different states?

    
There is no single nationwide answer, and courts have not resolved it uniformly. The commonly recommended, conservative practice — and the one this tool applies — is to require all-party consent whenever either state involved is an all-party state, because at least one court has applied the stricter state's law to protect a recipient there (Kearney v. Salomon Smith Barney, Inc., 39 Cal. 4th 95 (2006), applying California's law even though the recording company was based elsewhere). Treat this as the reason the conservative reading is conservative, not as a guarantee for every state pair.

    
Is this legal advice?

    
No. This is a reference lookup against a fixed table of each state's default rule, built from publicly available summaries of state wiretapping and eavesdropping statutes. It does not know the facts of your specific call, does not model exceptions (in-person conversations, 911 calls, law enforcement, a parent recording a minor's calls, industry-specific notice rules), and state statutes are amended and renumbered without notice. Verify the current statute text or ask a lawyer licensed in the relevant state before you rely on this for an actual call.

    
Is anything I type uploaded anywhere?

    
No. The two states you pick and the script you generate are looked up and rendered entirely in your browser from a fixed table shipped with the page. Nothing is sent anywhere. The CLI makes no network call either.

  


  

    
No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal advice, and it does not replace a qualified attorney licensed in the relevant state. It reports each state's default call-recording consent classification and a conservative combined reading for interstate calls — nothing more — and it does not model exceptions (in-person conversations, emergency calls, law enforcement, minors, industry-specific notice rules) or know the facts of your specific call. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, including checking the current statute text. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

    
Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get cli.mjs and run it yourself.

    
Everything runs in your browser. Nothing you type is ever uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (requirement_checked, script_generated, example_loaded, link_shared, link_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. The "Copy shareable link" button puts the two states and script fields into the link itself — nothing is sent to a server to generate it. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

    

    
Also worth a pass on the same repo: Consent Change Record covers a different consent problem entirely (cookie/tracking consent on a website, not call recording), Salary Range Posting Check is the same kind of US-state-law reference table and disclosure posture, applied to job-posting pay ranges instead, and Final Paycheck Deadline Calculator applies that same table-and-disclosure shape to a state's final-paycheck-timing deadline instead of a recording-consent rule. If you're comparing this to just looking each state up yourself, see how this compares to a manual state-by-state lookup.

    
Free and open source. If this saved you a compliance headache, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-checking-each-states-statute-by-hand..text:
← back to the checker

This checker vs. looking up each state's statute by hand

The usual way to answer "do I need consent to record this call?" is to search "is [state] one-party or two-party consent," read whichever page ranks first, and move on. That answers the single-state question well enough most of the time. It does not answer the question that actually matters for a remote sales, support, or recruiting team: a caller in one state and a recipient in another, which needs a combining rule and a citation to check, not two separate searches and a guess.

What each one is for

A one-off search is free and needs no tool: type the state name, read the first confident-sounding answer. It works fine when both parties are obviously in the same state and the page you land on happens to be right.

This checker looks up both states at once, applies a stated, cited combining rule for the interstate case (all-party consent whenever either state is one of the fourteen that requires it), names the precedent behind that conservative reading, and generates the actual words to say on the call — all from one fixed table rather than several searches under time pressure.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Is California an all-party-consent state?Either one. A single search answers this, and so does this checker.
A Texas caller phones a California recipient — whose rule controls?This checker. That needs a combining rule and a citation to the interstate precedent, not two separate single-state answers.
Does the search result I found mention Nevada's and Michigan's known ambiguity, or just state a flat answer?Often neither notices; this checker discloses both explicitly rather than picking a confident-sounding side.
What do I actually say to the other party once I know the rule?This checker's disclosure-script generator. A search result tells you the rule, not the words.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?Neither. A search involves no tool of ours at all, and this checker runs entirely in your browser.

Common questions

Isn't searching "is [state] one-party or two-party consent" enough?

It answers the single-state question, and plenty of free pages already answer it correctly. What it does not answer on its own is the interstate case — a caller in one state and a recipient in another — which needs a combining rule, not just two separate lookups, and which is exactly where the conservative all-party guidance and its supporting precedent matter.

What does a one-off search not give you that this tool does?

Three things bundled together: the combined requirement for a specific pair of states in one step, the exact statute citation to check against the current text, and a ready-to-read disclosure script for the call opening — rather than three separate searches and a script you write yourself under time pressure.

Why is stopping at the first search result risky here?

Because several states carry a real, disclosed ambiguity — Nevada's statute reads as one-party but its Supreme Court has applied it as all-party; Michigan's courts have gone different ways depending on who is recording. A page that states a flat answer with no caveat may simply not mention the ambiguity, and a reader has no way to tell confident from correct without checking a second source.

Does this replace reading the actual statute?

No, and it says so on every page. It points you at the exact statute citation for the fourteen all-party states so the next step is reading that specific section, not a general search that may surface an outdated summary.

No warranty. This page and the linked checker are provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. They are not legal advice, and they do not replace a qualified attorney licensed in the relevant state. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying the output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

This page names no specific product. "Looking up each state's statute by hand" describes a manual habit anyone can do with a search engine, not any company's product or service.

Nothing leaves your browser. The checker this page links to runs entirely client-side; nothing you enter is uploaded anywhere.

why-call-recording-consent-laws-differ-b.text:
← Back to Call Recording Consent Check

Why call recording consent laws differ by state

The federal Wiretap Act (18 U.S.C. § 2511(2)(d)) only ever set a floor: a person who is a party to a call — or who has the prior consent of one party — may record it, unless the recording is for a criminal or tortious purpose. That is a one-party-consent rule, and it is the default everywhere in the US unless a state has legislated something stricter. Fourteen states and DC did: California, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Montana, Nevada, New Hampshire, Oregon, Pennsylvania, and Washington all require every party's consent before a call may be recorded — usually enacted as part of a broader eavesdropping or wiretapping statute concerned with privacy in one's own communications generally, not call recording specifically.

Two states with a genuinely disclosed ambiguity

Most of the fourteen are unambiguous in their own statute text. Two are not, and this tool names both rather than smoothing them into a clean answer:

StateWhat the statute text saysHow it is actually applied
NevadaReads as one-party consent (Nev. Rev. Stat. § 200.620)The Nevada Supreme Court in Lane v. Allstate Ins. Co., 969 P.2d 938 (Nev. 1998) interpreted it to require all-party consent — this tool follows the applied reading, not the bare text
MichiganMich. Comp. Laws § 750.539c, arguably one-party for a participant recording their own callMichigan appellate decisions have gone the other way for a recording by someone not a party to the call. This tool lists Michigan as all-party out of caution and calls it the least certain classification in the table

The interstate case: whose rule applies?

No federal court has resolved this uniformly for every pairing of states, and this tool does not pretend otherwise. The commonly recommended, conservative practice is to apply the stricter rule whenever either party is in an all-party state — and at least one state's highest court has done exactly that: Kearney v. Salomon Smith Barney, Inc., 39 Cal. 4th 95 (2006) applied California's all-party rule to protect California call recipients even though the recording company was based out of state. That is the reasoning this tool's conservative guidance rests on — a real precedent for the direction it recommends, not a guarantee that every state pair resolves the same way.

What this tool checks, and what it deliberately doesn't

CheckSourceOut of scope
Per-state default classificationA fixed table of each state's own wiretapping/eavesdropping statute (all-party states cite the specific section; one-party states point to the federal baseline)Verifying the statute hasn't been amended since this table was built — state law changes without notice
Interstate combining ruleConservative all-party guidance whenever either state requires it, citing the Kearney precedent for whyA guarantee that every state pair resolves this way in every court — no such uniform rule exists
Disclosure scriptA ready-to-read call-opening line matching the determined requirementIndustry-specific notice rules (some insurance and financial-services regulators require their own disclosure) and any language beyond English

Also out of scope entirely: in-person conversations (several all-party states, Oregon among them, treat these differently from phone or electronic calls), 911 and emergency calls, law-enforcement recording, and a parent's vicarious consent to record a minor child's calls.

Wiring the classification into an onboarding or CI step

Check a new sales region or call-routing rule before it ships:

node ventures/call-recording-consent-check/cli.mjs check Texas California
node ventures/call-recording-consent-check/cli.mjs script all-party --company "Acme Inc." --purpose "training purposes"

check exits 1 when the pair requires all-party consent, so it can gate a new market's onboarding checklist the same way any other compliance CLI check does.

Common questions

Why do only some states require all-party consent?

The federal Wiretap Act only ever set a floor — one party's consent is enough unless the recording is for a criminal or tortious purpose — and left states free to require more. Fourteen states and DC did, usually framed around a broader right to privacy in one's own communications rather than call recording specifically; the other thirty-six left the federal floor as their own rule.

Which states have a genuinely disclosed ambiguity rather than a clean answer?

Two, named explicitly in this tool's own table rather than smoothed over. Nevada's statute reads as one-party consent, but the Nevada Supreme Court in Lane v. Allstate Ins. Co. (1998) interpreted it to require all-party consent, and it is enforced that way. Michigan's statute text is read by some courts as one-party for a participant recording their own call, while other Michigan appellate decisions have gone the other way for a non-party's recording — this table lists Michigan as all-party out of caution, and says so.

What actually happens on a call between two different states?

No federal court has settled this uniformly for every state pair. The commonly recommended, conservative practice is to apply the stricter (all-party) rule whenever either party is in an all-party state, and at least one state supreme court has done exactly that for a call reaching its own residents (Kearney v. Salomon Smith Barney, Inc., 39 Cal. 4th 95 (2006)). This tool follows that conservative reading rather than assuming the recording party's own state always controls.

What does this tool deliberately not check?

In-person conversations (several all-party states, Oregon among them, treat these differently from phone or electronic calls), 911 and emergency calls, law-enforcement recording, a parent's vicarious consent to record a minor child's calls, and any industry-specific notice rule (some insurance and financial-services regulators require their own disclosure separate from the wiretap statute). It also does not verify that a state's statute hasn't been amended since this table was built.

No warranty. This page and the tool it documents report each state's default call-recording consent classification and a conservative combined reading for interstate calls — nothing more. It is not legal advice and does not know the facts of your specific call. State statutes are amended and renumbered without notice; verify the current text or ask a lawyer licensed in the relevant state before relying on this. Back to the tool.
